0.0.n: Refers to the place where the speaker and others are gathered.

0.1.n: Marks the location where people are present.

0.2.n: いる describes living beings and modifies みんな here: the people who are here.

0.3.n: Refers to all the people present.

0.4.n: Includes everyone here among those who had this kind of dream.

0.5.n: With ような, it describes similarity rather than necessarily an exact match.

0.6.n: よう combines with 同じ and な to describe a similar kind of dream.

0.7.n: Links よう to the noun 夢 in the expression 同じような.

0.8.n: 夢を見る is the usual Japanese expression for having a dream while asleep.

0.9.n: Marks 夢 as what was experienced with 見た.

0.10.n: Past form of 見る; with 夢, it means experiencing a dream rather than literally seeing something.

0.11.n: Short for の; introduces the speaker’s realization in んだ.

0.12.n: Plain statement ending that completes the explanatory expression んだ.

0.13.n: Seeks agreement or shares a realization with the listener.

1.0.n: A family name; Japanese names normally place the family name first.

1.1.n: A given name; together with 桜島, it identifies Mai Sakurajima.

1.2.n: Marks Mai Sakurajima as the person making the disclosure.

1.3.n: A family name, paired here with the given name 透子.

1.4.n: A given name; together with 霧島, it identifies Touko Kirishima.

1.5.n: Combines だ, stating identity, with quotation marker って to introduce what she reveals.

1.6.n: An English loanword used here for publicly revealing a hidden identity, not necessarily sexuality.

1.7.n: Makes カミングアウト into a verb; the whole phrase describes the dream’s content.

1.8.n: The preceding clause tells us what happens in this dream.

2.0.n: Names the people who share this hope; no subject particle is spoken here.

2.2.n: A title or platform name here, literally meaning to dream.

2.4.n: Marks where the text was written or posted.

2.5.n: Past passive form of 書く: the focus is on what was written, not who wrote it.

2.6.n: Follows 書かれた to express matching what was written.

2.7.n: Links 通り to なる, showing how events are expected to turn out.

2.8.n: Describes events coming to match what was written.

2.9.n: Turns the preceding clause into something that can be hoped for.

2.10.n: Marks the entire こと phrase as what everyone hopes for.

2.11.n: Shortened from 望んでいる, expressing an ongoing wish.

2.12.n: Short for の, introducing an explanation or realization.

2.13.n: Completes んだ, presenting the speaker’s interpretation of everyone’s wishes.

2.14.n: Adds a reflective tone, as though the speaker is thinking aloud.

3.0.n: Softens the transition to the speaker’s next thought.

3.1.n: This is the first part of でも, which functions as one connecting word here.

3.2.n: Completes でも; it does not independently mean also in this line.

3.4.n: A given name, referring to Mai Sakurajima.

3.5.n: Adds polite respect to Mai’s name without specifying marital status.

3.6.n: Marks Mai as the person expected to deny the claim.

3.7.n: An English loanword naming the place where Mai will speak.

3.8.n: Marks the location where the denial will take place.

3.9.n: Emphasizes that Mai will give a clear, adequate denial.

3.10.n: 否定する becomes 否定して plus くれる, presenting the denial as helpful to the speaker or their group.

3.11.n: Expresses a confident expectation, not an obligation.

3.12.n: Completes はずだ, stating what the speaker expects.

3.13.n: Gives the expected denial as the reason for the conclusion that follows.

3.15.n: Refers back to the fuss surrounding the identity claim.

3.16.n: Describes the public fuss or excitement about the situation.

3.17.n: Adds the commotion to what will be resolved by the denial.

3.18.n: Names the day when the commotion is expected to end.

3.19.n: Marks today as the endpoint of the commotion.

3.20.n: A noun meaning an ending, used here to say the commotion will be finished.

3.21.n: Casual quotation marker introducing the conclusion summarized by こと.

3.22.n: In ってことだ, it presents what follows logically from the preceding situation.

3.23.n: Completes ってことだ, stating the speaker’s conclusion.

3.24.n: Gives the conclusion a reflective, thinking-aloud tone.

0.lit: Everyone who is here also had a similar kind of dream, it turns out, huh.
0.tip: 夢を見る literally says see a dream, but naturally means have a dream.

1.lit: A dream in which Mai Sakurajima reveals that she is Touko Kirishima.
1.tip: Japanese puts the entire description before 夢, rather than adding a clause after dream.

2.lit: Everyone is hoping for things to turn out exactly as written on Yumemiru, huh.
2.tip: A clause plus こと turns an event into something you can wish for, marked here by を.

3.lit: Well, but Mai should properly deny it for us onstage, so that commotion too ends today, meaning, huh.
3.tip: はずだ expresses confident expectation: the speaker expects Mai’s denial but is not reporting it as an established fact.
